title: Chemical Bonding
description: Ionic, covalent, and metallic bonds — how and why atoms join together.

notes.heading: Ionic Bonding
notes.body: Electrons transfer from metal to non-metal. Metal loses electrons → positive ion (cation). Non-metal gains electrons → negative ion (anion). Opposite charges attract. Example: Na loses 1 electron to Cl → Na⁺Cl⁻ (sodium chloride). Forms giant lattice with high melting point.

notes.heading: Covalent Bonding
notes.body: Atoms share pairs of electrons. Typically between two non-metals. One shared pair = single bond. Example: H₂O — each H shares one pair with O. O₂ has a double bond (two shared pairs). Simple molecular substances have low melting points.

notes.heading: Metallic Bonding
notes.body: Metal atoms release outer electrons into a "sea of electrons." Positive metal ions held by attraction to free-moving (delocalised) electrons. This explains: conductivity (electrons move), malleability (layers slide), high melting point (strong attractions).

flashcards.definition: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions from electron transfer.
Atoms sharing a pair of electrons.
flashcards.example: H₂O: H shares electrons with O.

flashcards.definition: Atom that has lost or gained electrons, giving it a charge.
Lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.
Electrons not attached to a single atom — free to move throughout a metal.

questions.stem: Electron transfer from metal to non-metal creates:
questions.explanation: Ionic bonding involves electron transfer; the ions then attract.
Made of two non-metals (H and O), so they share electrons in covalent bonds.

questions.stem: Sodium (1 outer electron) in ionic bonding will:
questions.explanation: Metals lose electrons; Na loses its 1 outer electron → Na⁺.
Delocalised electrons flow through the metal lattice as current.
Strong electrostatic forces in giant lattice → high melting points.
